conversation_logs.strength_noted: Her cold-call is genuinely warm — she names the student, waits, and nobody flinches. The wait time is longer than mine by a mile.
conversation_logs.more_frequently: Turn-and-talk before the whole-group share. Students arrived at the share with something already formed.
conversation_logs.less_frequently: She re-explains after a correct answer, which quietly tells the class the answer needed her endorsement.
conversation_logs.resources: She is sending me her discussion-protocol one-pager. I owe her the unit map for the ratios arc.
conversation_logs.vision: Ava wants the room to run on student talk, with her voice as the smallest one in it.

conversation_logs.strength_noted: He can restart a dead room in about ninety seconds. Students track him and the pace never sags.
conversation_logs.more_frequently: Write the objective where students can see it. Twice I watched a kid get lost and have nothing to steer back toward.
conversation_logs.less_frequently: Multi-step verbal directions during transitions. Three instructions at once and a third of the room is guessing.
conversation_logs.resources: I said I would share the checkpoint slide I use mid-lesson. He is going to try it Thursday.
conversation_logs.vision: Liam is trying to get the energy of his best days to show up on the ordinary ones.

conversation_logs.strength_noted: His daily objectives are written as questions students can actually answer by the bell. No fluff, no verbs like "explore".
conversation_logs.more_frequently: The five-minute recap at the start that reconnects yesterday to today. It did more than any review day would have.
conversation_logs.less_frequently: Two new representations in one lesson. The second one landed on students still holding the first.
conversation_logs.resources: Swapping unit maps. He wants my pacing calendar; I want his objective-writing frame.
conversation_logs.vision: Noah wants a unit where every day obviously earns its place in the arc.

conversation_logs.strength_noted: The exit ticket is three questions and she has the reteach list before she leaves the room. No weekend grading.
conversation_logs.more_frequently: Showing students the rubric row she is actually scoring. They stopped guessing at what "developing" meant.
conversation_logs.less_frequently: Written comments on work that will be revised anyway. She agreed most of it is never read.
conversation_logs.resources: She is giving me the exit-ticket template. I am walking her through how I do the revision cycle.
conversation_logs.vision: Avery is rebuilding the feedback loop so it closes in a day instead of a week.

conversation_logs.strength_noted: He keeps a two-line log of every family call. When a hard conversation comes, he has history to stand on.
conversation_logs.more_frequently: Naming the specific thing the student did, not the trait. "She revised the whole second paragraph" travels better than "she is conscientious".
conversation_logs.less_frequently: Apologising at the start of a call. It sets the family up to expect bad news before he has said anything.
conversation_logs.resources: He is sharing his call log format. I am sending him the repair conversation script we use after a conflict.
conversation_logs.vision: Mason wants the first contact home to be about something good, before anything has gone wrong.

conversation_logs.strength_noted: She repairs fast. A student pushed back hard and they were fine four minutes later, with no audience to the reset.
conversation_logs.more_frequently: The private check-in at the door. Two kids walked in already regulated because of a ten-second conversation.
conversation_logs.less_frequently: Addressing one student's behaviour to the whole room. The other twenty-nine pay for it and the one it is aimed at digs in.
conversation_logs.resources: I am borrowing her door check-in. She wants the norms-setting activity I run in September.
conversation_logs.vision: Harper wants the class norms to hold without her having to enforce them out loud.

profiles.inspiration: I stopped teaching and immediately missed the only part that mattered: watching somebody get better at something hard.
Math was the first subject where I felt genuinely smart, and only because someone slowed down for me. I keep the pace slow on purpose.
I like the moment a student stops asking whether they got it right and starts asking why it works.
Nobody in my family had done a science degree. A teacher handed me a lab notebook and acted like it was obvious I'd use it.
The best lesson I ever taught was one I scrapped halfway through, because the students had a better question than mine.
Every family I call is braced for bad news. I try to make the first call the one that isn't.
A class that laughs together will argue about a book together. I have never found a shortcut around that order.
I had a teacher who ran class like a conversation you couldn't wait to join. I've been chasing that room ever since.
I spent my first three years grading until midnight and calling it dedication. Now I'd rather design the unit so the feedback is fast and the kids actually read it.
I teach the kid who has already decided they are not a reader. That decision gets made early and it is almost always wrong.

survey_items.text: When a lesson isn't working, there's a specific colleague I can go to.
In the past month, at least one colleague has come to me for help with their teaching.
The people I turn to for help teach different subjects or grades than I do.
I regularly talk with colleagues about the actual work of teaching, not just logistics.
When I have a hard teaching problem, I mostly work it out on my own.
I've built a new working relationship with a colleague this year.
I feel like a full member of this faculty, not a guest in it.
There are people here who would notice and care if I left.
I can tell a colleague that a lesson failed without it being held against me.
When I've tried something new and it flopped, I've felt supported, not judged.
There are colleagues I'd never be fully honest with about my teaching.
When I've raised a real concern, I've seen it lead to something.
My expertise gets used in decisions here, not just my compliance.
The work I do here connects to something I actually believe in.
I share a sense of mission with the colleagues I work most closely with.
The teachers I work with and I share a common language for what good teaching looks like.
If we compared, my colleagues and I would largely agree on what makes a lesson excellent.
When we look at student work together, we're using the same standards.
I could name what this school is trying to accomplish this year.
The goals leadership talks about and the goals I care about are the same goals.
Good practice here stays private; we each just figure it out alone.
I've seen this staff solve a problem together that none of us could have solved alone.
Working together, the teachers here can reach even our most disengaged students.
When a student is struggling, we're good at changing course as a group.
Whether a kid succeeds here comes down to which teacher they got, not us as a staff.
I'm confident this faculty can improve outcomes for our hardest-to-teach students.
